title: Needs, wants and the line between
blurb: Asha has {income} a month and a list of things to pay for. Learn how to sort needs from wants, and why the line moves.
t1.title: Needs and wants
t1.hook: Asha earns {income} a month from tutoring. Her list this month: a bus pass {bus}, lunch {food}, new sneakers {sneakers} and a movie {movie}. What should she pay first?
t1.define: A **need** is something you must have to live, study or earn. A **want** is nice to have, but you can live without it.
t1.analogy: Think of a thali. Dal and roti fill you up: those are the needs. The sweet on the side is lovely, but you can eat well without it. That is a want.
q1.prompt: Which item on Asha's list is a need?
q1.hint: Which one helps her keep earning?
q1.explain: Without the bus pass she cannot reach her students. The sneakers and the movie can wait.
q1.opt.a: The bus pass to reach her students
q2.prompt: Her two needs are the bus pass and lunch. What do they cost together? Type a number in rupees.
t2.title: The in-between
t2.define: Many things sit **in between**. A phone is a need for a student who studies online. A very costly phone is mostly a want.
t2.note: Look closely at the item. The need is often the basic version. The fancy extras are the want.
q3.prompt: Meena needs a phone to join her online coaching. Which part of a fancy phone is the want?
q3.hint: A basic phone already joins the class.
q3.explain: A basic phone meets the need. The extras that push the price up are the want.
q3.opt.a: Being able to join her classes
q3.opt.b: The extras that make it cost more
q3.opt.c: The whole phone, because phones are wants
q3.fb.c: A phone is not all one thing. A basic one meets the need, and only the extras are the want.
q3.opt.d: Nothing, a phone is always a need
q4.prompt: A basic phone that joins classes costs {basicPhone}. The fancy one costs {fancyPhone}. How many rupees of the fancy phone are the want? Type a number.
q4.hint: The want is the extra: fancy price minus basic price.
t3.title: The line moves
t3.define: The line between need and want is not the same for everyone. It moves with your work, your home and your life.
t3.steps.1: Ask: what happens if I do not have it?
t3.steps.2: Ask: is there a cheaper way to meet the same need?
t3.steps.3: Ask: can it wait a month or two?
q5.prompt: Ravi sells vegetables from a cart far from home. Asha lives next to her college. Why can a scooter be a need for Ravi but a want for Asha?
q5.hint: Think about what each person uses it for.
q5.explain: Needs depend on a person's life. The same scooter helps one person earn and is a treat for another.
q5.opt.b: It cannot be: a need is a need for everyone
q5.fb.b: Needs depend on a person's life. The same scooter can help one person earn and be a treat for another.
q5.opt.c: Because it depends on their work and where they live
q5.opt.d: Because shops decide what is a need
t4.title: Lab: where does the month go?
t4.explore: Open the lab. Move the sliders for needs and wants and watch what is left of the month.
q6.prompt: In the lab, set needs to {n2} and wants to {w2}. How much is left from the month? Type a number.
q6.hint: Read the Left over box in the lab.
q7.prompt: Needs are {n3} and wants are {w3} on an income of {income}. What does this plan say?
q7.hint: Add the two, then compare with the income.
q7.explain: {n3} plus {w3} is more than {income}. Something has to give.
q7.opt.a: She has money left to save
q7.opt.b: She plans to spend more than she earns
t5.title: Wants are not bad
t5.misconception: Many teenagers think good money habits mean cutting every want. That is not the point. A planned want is fine. The trouble starts when a want eats the money for needs.
t5.tradeoff: Pay needs first. Then give wants a fixed place in the month. Wants you planned for feel better than wants you feel guilty about.
q8.prompt: Ravi says: cut every want and you will be fine. What is the best reply?
q8.hint: Think about whether a plan with no fun is easy to follow.
q8.explain: A plan that pays needs first and keeps a small, fixed share for wants is easier to follow.
q8.opt.a: He is right: wants are wasteful
q8.fb.a: Wants are not wasteful. A small planned want keeps a plan easy to follow. The risk is wants that crowd out needs.
q8.opt.b: Pay needs first, and plan a small place for wants
q8.opt.c: Pay for wants first, needs later
q8.opt.d: Wants and needs are the same thing
q9.prompt: What share of her income do Asha's needs take? Type a percentage.
q9.hint: Divide her needs total by her income, then write it as a percentage.
t6.title: Challenge
t6.formula: Share of income = amount ÷ income. A cap in rupees = income × the share you allow.
q10.prompt: Asha decides her wants may take at most {capShare} of her income. How many rupees is that? Type a number.
glossary.plan_need.def: Something you must have to live, study or earn.
glossary.plan_want.def: Something nice to have that you can live without.
